cards.explanation: The answer is that they rise up and rebuild God's house. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak “…rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) The prophets spoke, and these two got moving. Work boots on, friends.

The answer is False. The text says the prophets of God were with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, helping them. (Ezra 5:2) It doesn't spell out how they helped, but they were right there in the work. I think a builder feels braver with a prophet at his elbow.

The answer is who authorized them to rebuild. Tattenai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, asks, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (Ezra 5:3) That's the big question of the whole passage, friends. He wants to know who gave the okay.

The answer is names. Tattenai's crew asks, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (Ezra 5:4) They want to know who's doing the work, bakers. Not just the work, the workers.

The answer is False. The text says the elders “…were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.” (Ezra 5:5) The governor asked his questions, and the elders were not stopped. A governor shows up with questions, and still they aren't stopped.

The answer is their God's. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5) That's why they weren't stopped, friends. A governor was asking questions, and God's eye was on them. The text doesn't say anything fancy about how, only that His eye was on them.

The answer is True. Tattenai tells King Darius, “This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands.” (Ezra 5:8) He's the one asking all the questions, and he still writes that down. The man came to question the builders and ended up writing them a glowing report, bakers.

The answer is servants of the God of heaven and earth. The elders answer, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11) Tattenai had asked who authorized the rebuilding, and this is how they begin their answer, friends. Not a title, not a name drop, just who they serve.

The answer is king. The elders say they're rebuilding the temple “…a great king of Israel built and completed.” (Ezra 5:11) The text doesn't name him here. The point, bakers, is it was a real temple with a real history, and they weren't starting from nothing.

The answer is that their fathers angered the God of heaven. The elders say, “…since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezra 5:12) Nebuchadnezzar is the Chaldean who destroyed the temple. I think it takes some guts to say that out loud to a governor, friends, but the elders say it plainly.

The answer is King Cyrus. The elders say, “In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.” (Ezra 5:13) That little word “however” is where the story turns, bakers. After the hard part comes the hopeful part.

The answer is Sheshbazzar. Cyrus gave the gold and silver articles “…to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor” (Ezra 5:14) A governor's title and all those gold and silver articles, friends. That's a lot to get from Cyrus, Sheshbazzar.

The answer is True. The elders quote Cyrus telling Sheshbazzar, “Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.” (Ezra 5:15) Same site, the very same spot, bakers. The instructions were clear.

The answer is foundation. The elders say Sheshbazzar “…came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem…” (Ezra 5:16) That's where it all started, friends. A building has to begin somewhere, and this one began at the bottom.

The answer is False. The elders say, “…from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.” (Ezra 5:16) The work has been going since the foundation was laid, and it's still in progress. They don't oversell it to the governor, bakers.

The answer is archives. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:17) He wants it checked in the records, friends. He's asking for the search, then waiting on the king's decision. If the king says yes, somebody gets a dusty job. The story isn't over yet.
